record.label: Existence, coupling and uniqueness of the controlled diffusion
record.statement: For every gamma in U in the stated zero-field normalization and a fixed standard Brownian system, dX_t=gamma(t)Phi_x(t,X_t)dt+dB_t, X_0=0, has a unique strong solution through time 1. Solutions for L1 coefficient and smooth-terminal approximants driven by the same Brownian motion converge uniformly on compact strips below 1. Every associated diffusion in the selected formal model agrees almost surely with the constructed diffusion for every time in [0,1].
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. Same Brownian system, coefficient and control value throughout; uniqueness permits later transfer of moment identities to any associated diffusion. Pathwise coupling and existence are source-level analytic packages, not an observed build.

aligned_passages.text: ### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. The strip estimates justify the interior calculations and finite meshes; the terminal bound and integrability justify the later endpoint limits. The two roles must remain separate. Their uses depend on the region and limit. On a fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<1$, bounded spatial derivatives and locally absolutely continuous time dependence justify the Itô identities and Euler coupling. Across a jump of $\gamma$, the spatial derivative moments remain continuous and the time equations hold almost everywhere; this is enough for contact slopes and the endpoint chord comparison. Inside a constant interval, classical time differentiation permits the strict-curvature calculation. As $T\uparrow1$, the controls change: the displayed value bound, integrable coefficient tails and martingale convergence justify first variation and terminal value. No differentiated estimate at the terminal cusp is used. These are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1 and its diffusion consequences][fs-reg]; [§2.4](#strip-estimates) reconstructs their uniformity. The hypotheses also have distinct uses. Zero field supplies evenness, $u(0,0)=0$ and reflection in the shape argument. The convention $\xi''=1$ fixes the curvature coefficients. Monotonicity gives bounded coefficients before time one and nonnegative coefficient jumps; it also turns a support gap into a constant interval. Integrability controls terminal tails and Fubini interchanges, while local finiteness of the Stieltjes measure is enough for compact mass removal. Minimality first enters through the variational inequality in §3; the constant-interval curvature estimate itself applies to an admissible coefficient without assuming it is a minimiser. [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]; [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), §6][fs-var]. ### 2.3 Which prior results play which role The imported ground-state formula supplies two facts with different uses. Auffinger and Chen's Theorem 1 identifies the ground-state limit with an infimum over $\mathcal U$. To choose a coefficient attaining that infimum, one must also use their construction in the proof of Lemma 3. In the cited arXiv v2, the theorem is on p. 3, the compactness construction is on pp. 7–9, and the lower-bound proof is on pp. 11–12. Here is the part of that construction which supplies the witness. Let $\alpha_\beta$ be a positive-temperature Parisi distribution function. The source bounds $\beta\alpha_\beta(t)$ uniformly on each interval ending before one. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence produce a nonnegative, nondecreasing right-continuous limit $\gamma_0$. In the SK normalization, the source's weighted integral bound also controls $\int_0^1\beta\alpha_\beta(t)\,dt$. For every nonnegative nondecreasing $h$, splitting at $1/2$ gives $\int_0^1 h(t)\,dt\le4\int_0^1t h(t)\,dt$: the first half is bounded by $h(1/2)/2$, and on the second half $t\ge1/2$. Fatou's lemma then gives $\gamma_0\in\mathcal U$. Mass can concentrate at time one during this limit, so compact convergence alone does not identify the limiting control problem. Write the limiting measure of the time coefficients as $$ \nu_0(dt)=\gamma_0(t)\,dt+m\delta_1(dt),\qquad m\geq0. $$ For an arbitrary admissible control, let $S$ denote its terminal state with coefficient $\gamma_0$. To see why the terminal choice is admissible, let the original control be $\alpha$ and put $S_s=B_s+\int_0^s\gamma_0(r)\alpha_r\,dr$. For a cutoff $\tau<1$ use $\alpha_s$ before $\tau$ and $g_k(S_s)$ afterwards, where $g_k$ is a continuous function bounded by one and converging pointwise to the sign with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=1$. This control uses only information available at time $s$. At fixed $\tau,k$, first take the temperature limit; then let $\tau\uparrow1$ and $k\to\infty$. The continuous terminal evaluation has thereby approached $\operatorname{sgn}(S)$ without anticipating a future state. The endpoint atom then contributes $$ |S+m\operatorname{sgn}(S)|-|S|=m $$ to the reward and $$ \tfrac12m\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(S)^2+1\bigr)=m $$ to the combined control and Parisi penalties. These contributions cancel. Taking the supremum over the remaining controls proves $P_*\geq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)$. The upper bound proved earlier in that paper gives $P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$. Therefore $$ P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma) \leq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)\leq P_*. $$ Thus $\gamma_0$ attains the infimum. The cancellation is a step in the imported existence proof; it is not an additional assumption about the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma_0$. In particular, $\nu_0$ here is the limit of coefficient-times-Lebesgue measures, not the order parameter's Stieltjes measure. The two measures must not be identified. [Auffinger and Chen, arXiv:1606.05335v2, pp. 7–12][ac17]. The cited theorem is stated for the almost-sure normalized maximum. Its expected-value formulation used here follows from Gaussian concentration. For $L_n=n^{-1}\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma)$, the Lipschitz constant in the Gaussian couplings is $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$. Hence $L_n-\mathbb E L_n\to0$ in probability. Since the almost-sure limit is the deterministic Parisi value, the deterministic sequence $\mathbb E L_n$ has the same limit. The full-support theorem below remains conditional on a minimizer; neither of the selected formal interfaces constructs one. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, Introduction, ground-state formula and its footnote][fs-main]. Auffinger–Chen–Zeng's infinite support does not exclude an interior gap. Their terminal-plateau observation anticipates one endpoint obstruction; the argument below supplies the quantitative boundary-layer proof used here. The full-support manuscript develops a rational coercivity route and credits Chen's 2026 theorem for the same full-support conclusion and smooth absolute continuity. Chen's Proposition 4.2 has the conditional crossing form $q''(t)=0\Rightarrow q'''(t)>0$; the cited rational certificate gives $q'''(t)>0$ throughout a positive constant interval. These are different sufficient mechanisms, and this record makes no priority claim for full support. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1 and Remark 7][acz]; [Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 4.2][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The transformed density comparisons also have antecedents in Lopatto's positive-temperature analysis and Chen's zero-temperature analysis; the rational coercive identity is the different step in the full-support proof. Zhou's positive-temperature interval-support result applies near the critical temperature, whereas Lopatto's cited theorem covers the low-temperature zero-field phase. Neither transfers full Stieltjes support to zero temperature on its own: for the minimizers, $\beta\mu_\beta$ converges vaguely on $[0,1)$ to the zero-temperature Stieltjes measure, while the unscaled Parisi probability measures converge weakly on $[0,1]$ to $\delta_1$. These are different measures and topologies. Convergence without an interval-specific lower bound can lose support information. The direct zero-temperature gap proof below is therefore essential. [Chen (2026), Remarks 1.4–1.5][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. Two later editions sharpen the comparison without entering the pinned September proof. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, Proposition 5.1 and (5.8)–Corollary 5.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4), proves a conditional curvature crossing on a positive constant interval. Its integrating factor makes a transformed curvature derivative strictly increasing, so the associated contact derivative decreases and then increases; it does not assert an unconditional positive third derivative. [Lopatto, arXiv:2610.00127v1, Theorem 2.3 and §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00127v1), works at positive temperature and positive external field. Its comparison requires one-sided bounds on the coefficient before and after the chosen time, a moment inequality and a stationarity equality. The subsequent moment bootstrap yields smooth, strictly positive density on a nontrivial support interval; a singleton support is a separate case. Neither theorem removes the hypotheses of the zero-temperature argument below. Here is an explicit example of the information lost in such a limit. It concerns admissible measures, not Parisi minimizers. Put $g=\mathbf1_{[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1)}$ and $q_n=1-n^{-2}$, and for $n\ge2$ define $$ \mu_n(dt)=\frac{g(t)+n^{-1}}n\mathbf1_{[0,q_n]}(t)\,dt +\left(1-\frac1n\int_0^{q_n}(g(t)+n^{-1})\,dt\right)\delta_{q_n}(dt). $$ The continuous part has mass at most $(2/3+1/n)/n<1$, so these are probability measures with a positive endpoint atom. Their density is positive throughout $[0,q_n]$, giving $\operatorname{supp}\mu_n=[0,q_n]$. Their continuous mass tends to zero and $q_n\to1$, hence $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_1$ weakly on $[0,1]$. For a compactly supported continuous test function on $[0,1)$, the endpoint atom eventually lies outside its support. Consequently $n\mu_n\to g(t)\,dt$ vaguely there, although the limit vanishes on $(1/3,2/3)$. Even the cumulative coefficients converge in the topology used for the PDE: with $\gamma_n(t)=n\mu_n([0,t])$ and $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$, their difference is $t/n$ below $q_n$, and $\gamma_n=n$ on the terminal strip of length $n^{-2}$. Thus $$ \|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}\le\frac1{2n}+\frac1n\longrightarrow0. $$ Every $\gamma_n$ is admissible, but $d\gamma$ has an interior gap. Minimality and the gap argument supply information that these convergences alone do not. An atom added at time one is likewise invisible to the coefficient on $[0,1)$ and hence to its PDE and variational functional; the zero-temperature problem does not select an endpoint mass. Control and gradient-martingale methods have antecedents in [Auffinger–Chen](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-014-2254-z) and [Jagannath–Tobasco](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04398v4). A finite-temperature theorem with smooth terminal value $\log\cosh$ does not alone establish the result with terminal cusp $|x|$. The required compact-strip and terminal estimates are supplied in [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [Chen–Handschy–Lerman](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4) supplies earlier zero-temperature regularity, control and uniqueness results (Theorem 4 for uniqueness). This is distinct from the earlier finite-temperature uniqueness result of Auffinger and Chen. [Montanari](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10897v2) and [El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00904v1) inform normalised discretisation and optimisation. The particular shifted Gaussian coefficient identity used here is proved in [OpenAI (2026a), §7][fs-cons].

For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, the pure,
zero-field [Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) Hamiltonian][SK] is
$$
H_n(\sigma)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,
\qquad \sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n.
$$
The limiting ground-state energy per spin, with the maximisation
convention, is
$$
P_*:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$
The Parisi formula expresses $P_*$ as a minimum over nondecreasing
functions. Our subject is the structure of a minimiser: its increments
charge every interval of overlap scales below one, and in fact have
strictly positive density at each interior scale. The proof uses one
quantitative bound twice, first to exclude constant intervals and then,
after an approximation, to prove pointwise positivity.

For two configurations, their overlap is
$R(\sigma,\tau)=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$. It determines the
energy covariance: $\mathbb E[H_n(\sigma)H_n(\tau)]=nR^2/2-1/2$.
Thus the Gaussian law of the energies is encoded by the overlaps.
We use the covariance convention $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, so $\xi''=1$;
adding one independent centred Gaussian of
variance $1/2$ to every configuration's energy gives covariance
$n\xi(R)$ and leaves the expected maximum unchanged. This is the
normalisation of the ground-state Parisi formula of
[Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1][AC]. There are no higher-order
interactions and no external field.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of the nonnegative, nondecreasing,
right-continuous functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Define the locally finite Stieltjes
measure by
$$
\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t),\qquad 0\leq t<1.
$$
Thus $\mu_\gamma((s,t])=\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)$: the measure records
the increments of $\gamma$. A point mass (atom) of size $\gamma(0)$
is allowed at zero, and the total mass need not be finite or equal
to one. All support statements use the relative topology of $[0,1)$.
A support gap is a relatively open interval of positive length with
zero mass; the cumulative coefficient is constant on such an interval.

The Parisi functional $\mathcal P(\gamma)$ is defined using an
auxiliary value function $\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$, where $x\in\mathbb R$
is a spatial variable and $t$ is the overlap parameter, treated as
time in the equation. Write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$ and use subscripts
for partial derivatives. The backward equation, terminal condition
and functional are
$$
\Phi_t=-\tfrac12\bigl(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma(t)\Phi_x^2\bigr),
\qquad \Phi(1,x)=|x|,
\qquad
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\tfrac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$
The terminal value $|x|$ is the zero-temperature value of one spin
in a field $x$. For an integrable
coefficient, the PDE solution is interpreted by approximation from
bounded monotone coefficients. The exact control
definition and stability theorem are [OpenAI (2026a), §1 and
Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS]. To turn minimality of $\mathcal P$ into a
condition on $\gamma$, we use a random process whose gradient moment
measures the first-order cost of changing $\gamma$. Write $u=\Phi_x$ for the spatial gradient
and $a=\Phi_{xx}$ for its spatial derivative. Let $B$ be standard
Brownian motion and define the diffusion $X$ and the moment $q$ by
$$
dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t,\qquad X_0=0,
\qquad q(t)=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2].
$$
The discrepancy $q(t)-t$ enters the first variation of $\mathcal P$;
minimality will force $q(t)=t$ on the support of $\mu_\gamma$.
The SDE has a unique strong solution. All
stochastic calculations below take place on compact time intervals
ending before one, unless an endpoint limit is justified explicitly.

## 3. How a candidate receives its value

To rule out a candidate, we will look for an allowed change that lowers
its value. Adding mass at one scale changes the cumulative coefficient
at every later scale. We therefore need both a value for each candidate
and a way to compute the cost of that change. The auxiliary optimisation
below supplies the value; its response to the starting state will enter
the first-variation formula in Section 5.1.

### 3.1 First evaluate the zero coefficient

The variational problem assigns each $\gamma$ a value by a one-dimensional
auxiliary optimisation. Its final reward at state $x$ is $|x|$: this is
the best one-spin score $\max_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}x\sigma$.
First take $\gamma=0$, when only noise changes the state. The auxiliary
clock is chosen so that noise accumulated over an interval of length
$h$ has variance $h$, the variance of $\sqrt hZ$. Starting at
time $t$ in state $x$, the remaining noise is therefore distributed
as $\sqrt{1-t}Z$. The expected final reward is

$$
\Phi_0(t,x)=\mathbb E|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z|
=\int_{\mathbb R}|x+\sqrt{1-t}z|\varphi(z)\,dz.
$$

At $(t,x)=(0,0)$ this is the calculation already performed:
$\Phi_0(0,0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. At $t=1$ no noise remains and the
value is $|x|$. The function gives an expected payoff at a specified
starting state; it is not a probability density.

### 3.2 Allowing a response to the noise

For a general $\gamma$, a response can bias the future state, with a
quadratic cost. Here the overlap scale $t$ plays the role of time;
the path is auxiliary, not a motion of the spins.
The noise is **Brownian motion** $B$: a continuous random path starting
at zero. Its increments over disjoint time intervals are independent;
over an interval of length $h$, an increment has the same distribution
as the centred Gaussian $\sqrt h Z$.

A **control** $\alpha_s\in[-1,1]$ chooses a response at each time
using only noise already observed since the starting time. It can react
to the past but cannot use future increments. To see why this matters,
let a sign $W=\pm1$, each with probability $1/2$, be revealed after
a single choice $v\in[-1,1]$.
The expected score $|W+v|-v^2/2$ is $1-v^2/2$, maximised at $v=0$.
A choice $v=W$ would score $3/2$, but uses information unavailable at
the time of choice. The continuous control problem repeats decisions
with this same restriction; the finite example only illustrates that
restriction.

For a starting position $x$, the value is

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_\alpha\mathbb E\left[
\left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right|
-\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds
\right].
$$

Inside the absolute value, noise and the accumulated bias change the
state before its final reward is paid. The second integral is the cost.
The supremum chooses the best permitted rule; its formal information
condition is progressive measurability. Expectation now averages over
Brownian paths for a fixed $\gamma$, rather than over spin couplings.
At $\gamma=0$ both control terms vanish, recovering Section 3.1.

The **Parisi functional** subtracts an explicit correction from this
optimised value:

$$
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)
-\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$

The inner supremum chooses a response for fixed $\gamma$; the outer
problem minimises $\mathcal P$ over $\gamma$. The ground-state Parisi
formula and attainment give

$$
P_*=\min_{\gamma\text{ admissible}}\mathcal P(\gamma).
$$

Each candidate supplies an upper bound, and minimisation finds the
sharpest one. This equality and attainment are external inputs from
[Auffinger–Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and the proof of Lemma 3][auffinger-chen];
Gaussian concentration gives the expected-value form used here.
The no-gap theorem assumes a minimiser and proves a property of it.
The value $\mathcal P(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$ alone does not establish
that the zero candidate minimises.

### 3.3 The response, the state and the averaged square

First consider the value as a function of the starting state, holding
$t$ and $\gamma$ fixed; we also write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$.
For any permitted control, use the same
responses to each Brownian history at two starting states $x$ and $y$.
The costs are unchanged, and the triangle inequality bounds the change
in the terminal reward by $|x-y|$. Taking the supremum over controls gives

$$
|\Phi_\gamma(t,x)-\Phi_\gamma(t,y)|\le |x-y|.
$$

The value is also **convex**: between two states its graph lies at or
below the chord joining their values. Indeed,
each fixed-control payoff is an average of translated absolute-value
functions, hence convex. Its chord lies at or below the chord of the
best endpoint payoffs; taking the supremum preserves that upper bound.

[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity] supply spatial
differentiability below time one. Let $u(t,x)=\partial_x\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ be the slope
as the starting state changes. A small shift $\delta$ changes the
best expected payoff by approximately $u(t,x)\delta$. Write
$a(t,x)=\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ for the rate at which that
slope changes. The displayed bound gives $|u|\le1$, and convexity
gives $a\ge0$. These are spatial derivatives: time is held fixed.

For the zero coefficient, the slope can be computed directly. Put
$F_{\mathrm G}(z)=\Pr(Z\le z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\varphi(y)\,dy$.
Moving $x$
slightly raises $|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z|$ when the final state is positive
and lowers it when the final state is negative. Consequently

$$
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1.
$$

Differentiating the integral is legitimate: the difference quotients
of the absolute value are bounded by one, and the Gaussian has zero
probability of hitting its corner. Thus the slope is the probability
of a positive final state minus the probability of a negative one.

For general $\gamma$, the control theorem says that the slope response
attains the value. Its local optimisation has a simple algebraic reason:
at slope $u$, the gain from a response $v$ minus its quadratic cost is

$$
\gamma vu-\tfrac12\gamma v^2
=\tfrac12\gamma u^2-\tfrac12\gamma(v-u)^2.
$$

Since $\gamma\ge0$ and $|u|\le1$, $v=u$ attains its maximum.
The optimised contribution $\gamma u^2/2$ also explains why a squared
slope will enter the sensitivity to $\gamma$. The control theorem and
the first-variation formula in Section 5.1 make these connections rigorous; the square
completion alone does not justify differentiating an optimised value.
The zero-temperature control representation is in
[Auffinger–Chen, Corollary 2, equation (12), and the extension after (13)][auffinger-chen].

Following the slope response generates the random state

$$
X_t=B_t+\int_0^t\gamma(s)u(s,X_s)\,ds,\qquad X_0=0.
$$

This is the **associated diffusion**. The rule is called **feedback**
because it uses the slope at the currently reached state. With $\gamma$
and $u$ supplied, a short forward step of length $h$ from state $x$
at time $t$, with $t+h<1$, is approximated by

$$
x+h\gamma(t)u(t,x)+\sqrt h Z.
$$

The response is evaluated before the fresh independent noise $Z$ is
observed. This discrete approximation explains the order of operations;
the integral equation defines the continuous process. Its drift accumulates
through time, so even a jump of $\gamma$ does not make $X$ jump.

Fix $\gamma$, follow a path to $X_t$, evaluate the slope there, square
it, and average over paths. This defines a deterministic curve

$$
q(t):=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2].
$$

Here $\Phi_\gamma$ and $u$ are deterministic functions; $X_t$ and
the response evaluated at it are random. Squaring before averaging
retains the size of both positive and negative responses.

**A calculation at half time.** For $\gamma=0$, $X_t=B_t$ and
$B_{1/2}$ has the same distribution as $Z/\sqrt2$. We can average
over paths by grouping them according to the state reached. At half
time the reached state has density $e^{-x^2}/\sqrt\pi$. This density
describes its **law**, assigning probability to positions on the real line. The law has
total mass one even though the order-parameter measure $\mu_0$ is
zero. The two measures describe different objects.

Average $u_0(1/2,x)^2$ with this density. Substituting $x=z/\sqrt2$
gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_0(1/2)
&=\int_{\mathbb R}(2F_{\mathrm G}(z)-1)^2\varphi(z)\,dz\\
&=\int_0^1(2v-1)^2\,dv=\frac13,
\qquad v=F_{\mathrm G}(z),\quad dv=\varphi(z)\,dz.
\end{aligned}
$$

The response at zero is zero, but its mean square at the random state
is $1/3$. Thus $q(t)=t$ is not automatic. Although every control is
optimal at $\gamma=0$, $q_0$ uses the value slope $u_0$.
Section 7.1 uses the whole curve to find a feasible decrease of
$\mathcal P(0)$; a discrepancy at one time does not suffice.

**Question 2: change the time.** Still take $\gamma=0$ everywhere,
but now set $t=1/4$. What variance has the state accumulated, and
what variance remains in its future reward? Write the Gaussian integral
for $q_0(1/4)$ without evaluating it. Section 7.4 gives the answer.

The analytic facts needed in the proof are

$$
q\in C^1([0,1)),\qquad q(0)=0,\qquad 0\le q(t)\le1,
\qquad q'(t)=\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2].
$$

Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable, with derivatives at zero
from the right. In particular, $q'$ stays continuous across jumps of
$\gamma$. Spatial curvature controls the growth of the squared response.
These facts hold for every admissible candidate and follow from
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity]. They suffice for
the proof below together with the further inputs stated at their uses.
Section 7.2 explains the PDE and stochastic calculation behind them.
The next argument uses these stated properties of the deterministic
curve $q$ to test changes of the cumulative weight $\gamma$.

### 7.1 Why the zero candidate does not minimise

Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,
the state is $B_t$. Differentiating the slope once more gives

$$
X_t=B_t,\qquad
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi(1-t)}}e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}.
$$

A Gaussian integral gives
$\mathbb E e^{-B_t^2/(1-t)}=\sqrt{(1-t)/(1+t)}$. Substituting
into $q_0'=\mathbb E[a_0(t,B_t)^2]$ and integrating from zero yields

$$
q_0'(t)=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

This recovers the half-time value $1/3$. It also shows that
$q_0(t)\to1$ while $q_0'(t)\to\infty$: convergence of a function
at one does not bound its derivative there.
The constant direction $\eta=1$ is admissible and adds an atom at zero.
Its cost is

$$
D\mathcal P(0)[1]
=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
=\frac14-\frac1\pi<0.
$$

So a small positive constant coefficient improves the zero candidate.
This calculation uses the heat and variation formulas, not a minimiser
hypothesis; see also [Chen–Handschy–Lerman, proof of Theorem 6][chl-optimality].

### 7.2 The value equation and the moment identity

At $t=1$ there is no noise or response left to accumulate, so the value
is $|x|$. At earlier times it includes the best remaining response.
Its partial differential equation (PDE) runs backward from that final value:

$$
\partial_t\Phi_\gamma
=-\frac12\left(\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma
+\gamma(t)(\partial_x\Phi_\gamma)^2\right),
\qquad \Phi_\gamma(1,x)=|x|.
$$

With the spatial derivatives $u$ and $a$ defined in Section 3.3,
the equation expresses
a recursive choice: choose a response for a short first step, then
use the best continuation from the state reached. At a continuity
point of $\gamma$, this gives the formal first-order relation

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)
=\sup_{|v|\le1}\left\{
\mathbb E\Phi_\gamma(t+h,x+\gamma(t)vh+\sqrt hZ)
-\tfrac12\gamma(t)v^2h\right\}+o(h).
$$

Subtract the present value, divide by $h$, and Taylor-expand.
The identities $\mathbb EZ=0$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$ give

$$
0=\Phi_t+\tfrac12\Phi_{xx}
  +\sup_{|v|\le1}\gamma(t)(v\Phi_x-v^2/2).
$$

The square completion from Section 3.3 gives a supremum of
$\gamma u^2/2$, attained at $v=u$, and hence the stated PDE. This calculation explains the equation;
justifying the recursion and the Taylor expansion requires the
control representation and regularity results. See
[Auffinger–Chen, Theorem 2 and Corollary 2][auffinger-chen] for the zero-temperature
control formula and [Jagannath–Tobasco, Lemma 18][jt-control] for the
control method with finite-temperature terminal data. The extension after
Auffinger–Chen's Corollary 2 covers integrable coefficients. The regularity
used here is in
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity].

Itô's rule is the chain rule for Brownian paths. Along
$dX_t=b_t\,dt+dB_t$, the coefficient of $dt$ (the **drift**)
in a smooth $f(t,X_t)$ is
$f_t+b_tf_x+f_{xx}/2$, and its noise term is $f_x\,dB_t$.
Differentiate the PDE in $x$ and take $b_t=\gamma u$. The drift of
the slope cancels:

$$
du(t,X_t)
=\underbrace{(u_t+\gamma u u_x+u_{xx}/2)}_{0}\,dt
+a(t,X_t)\,dB_t.
$$

Thus $M_t=u(t,X_t)$ is a bounded **martingale**: its conditional
expected later value, given observations up to time $t$, is its present
value. Zero field gives symmetry and $M_0=u(0,0)=0$. Applying Itô's rule once more
to $M_t^2$ gives

$$
d(M_t^2)=2M_ta(t,X_t)\,dB_t+a(t,X_t)^2\,dt.
$$

The noise term has mean zero because its coefficient is nonanticipating
and bounded on each strip ending before one. Taking expectations and
integrating yields $q(t)=\int_0^t\mathbb E[a(s,X_s)^2]\,ds$,
which gives the asserted derivative. Since $\mathbb EM_t=0$,
$q(t)$ is also the variance of the slope response.

For each fixed $T<1$, the required spatial derivatives are bounded on
$[0,T]\times\mathbb R$, and step-coefficient and smooth-terminal
approximations justify the identities. The bounds depend on the coefficient
and strip. The PDE holds almost everywhere in time. These are not
bounds up to time one.
